primers: Think of AI as a family of techniques, not one machine. A spam filter recognizes a category; a route planner searches for a path; a language model generates text. Machine learning is the branch that learns patterns from examples rather than having every rule written by hand. Deep learning uses networks of many processing layers. Generative AI creates new content.||A chat product wraps a model in an interface, storage, tools, and permissions. The model may write a request to search the web; the application performs that search. Changing the model does not automatically change the application's access.

Supervised learning uses examples paired with target answers, such as emails labeled spam or not spam. Unsupervised learning looks for structure without those labels, such as grouping similar customers. Self-supervised learning creates a training task from the data itself: predicting a hidden word is one example.||Reinforcement learning improves decisions using rewards from interaction. A game-playing system can learn which moves lead to winning. These approaches can be combined across a model's lifecycle.

Classification chooses a category. Regression predicts a numerical value. Clustering finds groups. Anomaly detection flags unusual cases. Recommendation ranks candidates for a user. Forecasting predicts future observations using past information.||A simple rule can be better than a model when the rule is stable and exact. Calculating a tax subtotal does not require a language model; interpreting a messy customer request might benefit from one. Start with the task, then choose the technique.

A convincing demonstration shows that something worked for those inputs under those conditions. It does not establish that it works reliably for everyone. Ask which examples were selected, what failed, and what counted as success.||AGI has no single universally accepted operational definition. Consciousness is a different question from task performance. Keep observed capabilities separate from claims about what a system experiences or could someday do.

Training adjusts numerical parameters called weights. Inference uses those weights to process a new input. A checkpoint is a saved state of a model, often accompanied by other information needed to resume training.||Pretraining develops broad patterns from large datasets. Post-training adapts behavior for tasks such as following instructions. Telling a chat assistant your name supplies context; it does not ordinarily rewrite its weights.

A dataset is a collection of choices: what to collect, whom to represent, which labels to trust, and what to remove. Repeated or mislabeled examples can teach misleading patterns. Synthetic examples are generated data, and they still need verification.||Imagine training a support classifier using only easy English messages. Strong results on similar messages tell you little about ambiguous or multilingual requests. Data coverage is part of capability.

Training data teaches the model. Validation data helps select settings. Test data estimates performance after those choices are made. If nearly identical examples appear in all three sets, the test may reward memorization.||Overfitting happens when a model fits the training examples too specifically. Distribution shift means new inputs differ from the data used to develop it. Both can make impressive development results fail in practice.

A loss function provides a signal about how wrong a prediction is under the chosen objective. Backpropagation assigns credit to parameters; an optimizer uses that information to update them. The learning rate controls update size.||A batch is a group of examples processed together; an epoch is a pass through a dataset. Smaller training loss is useful evidence, but held-out performance determines whether the learning generalizes.

A neural network transforms input through layers into representations useful for a task. An embedding represents an item with numbers so relationships can be compared. The numbers are not a dictionary definition or a guarantee of factual meaning.||Different architectures organize information differently. Convolutional networks exploit local patterns; recurrent networks process sequences through state; transformers use attention. Architecture is a design choice, not a ranking by itself.

A tokenizer turns text into units a model can process. A common word may be one token while an unusual name becomes several pieces. Spaces, punctuation, code, and different languages affect the count.||Tokens determine input capacity and often usage costs. Never assume a fixed word-to-token conversion across languages. Special tokens can signal boundaries or roles, and the model expects the correct template.

Attention lets a position combine information from other positions. In 'the animal was tired because it ran,' relationships between words help represent what 'it' refers to. This is computation, not human awareness.||An encoder builds representations of input; a decoder can generate a sequence. Causal masking prevents a text-generating decoder from using future tokens during its prediction task. Positional information distinguishes different word orders.

A dense model generally uses its main parameter blocks for every token. A mixture-of-experts model routes tokens through selected expert blocks. The total parameter count can therefore differ greatly from the number active per token.||Hardware, routing, context, and software all affect cost. A model advertised with more parameters is not automatically better for your task. Likewise, a large supported context window does not prove reliable retrieval of every detail.

A text generator repeatedly selects a next token using the context so far. Greedy decoding chooses the highest-scoring option; sampling can choose among plausible alternatives. Temperature and top-p change selection behavior when supported.||Increasing variety is not the same as improving truth. Output limits and stop conditions determine when generation ends. Repeating a prompt may produce different results even when the intended task is unchanged.

Some models spend additional computation exploring or checking steps before returning an answer. Decomposing a problem and verifying intermediate results can help, but extra computation can also pursue a mistaken assumption.||A displayed explanation is evidence about what the system says, not a guaranteed recording of its internal computation. Evaluate the final claim using tests, sources, or independent calculations.

A hallucination is unsupported or incorrect generated content presented as an answer. It can be a made-up quotation, a nonexistent API, or an invented event. Fluent wording makes such errors easy to overlook.||Sycophancy is excessive agreement with the user. A useful assistant should sometimes challenge a premise or say it lacks evidence. Asking a leading question can expose this weakness.

Separate the claim from the evidence. A citation must exist and support the specific statement. A tool must have actually run successfully. A calculation should be reproducible.||When an answer fails, ask whether information was missing, retrieval was wrong, interpretation failed, or execution broke. Rephrasing the prompt cannot fix every category of failure.

Give the model a task, the relevant facts, constraints, and a definition of success. 'Summarize this for a beginner in three paragraphs, preserving the exceptions' is more testable than 'make this good.'||Few-shot prompting supplies examples of desired behavior. Include difficult cases, not only easy ones. Separating source text from instructions reduces ambiguity, though formatting alone is not a security boundary.

Context is what the model receives for the current request. It may include your message, earlier messages, application instructions, retrieved documents, and tool results. All of this competes for finite capacity.||The interface may display history that is no longer included in full. Applications can omit or summarize earlier messages. A larger window helps capacity but does not guarantee that every detail influences the answer correctly.

Persistent memory is information stored outside the model and potentially supplied later. It can record a preference or a previous project decision. Working context is the information supplied now. Weights are learned parameters.||Memory needs provenance and updates. An old address remembered confidently can be worse than no address. A good design allows corrections and distinguishes stable preferences from temporary instructions.

Context engineering decides what information reaches the model and when. Relevant, current, well-labeled material often helps more than a large pile of unrelated text.||A handoff should preserve goals, constraints, decisions, evidence, and open questions. Summarization trades detail for space; test whether the compressed version still supports the next task.

A base model is trained to model data; an instruction-tuned variant is adapted to follow requests. Embedding models represent inputs for comparison, while rerankers score relevance among candidates. A vision-language model also accepts visual information.||These are different roles. A strong chat model may not be the best retrieval model. Choose according to the operation you need, not a shared family name.

A model card is the closest thing to a product specification for a checkpoint. Look for intended tasks, languages, limitations, license, evaluation setup, and supported input format. Missing information should remain unknown.||Check the exact revision and runtime requirements. A benchmark without its dataset, prompting method, or comparison baseline is difficult to interpret.

Weights contain learned parameters. A tokenizer describes how input becomes tokens. Configuration describes architecture and other settings. A chat template turns messages into the sequence the model expects.||Safetensors and GGUF are file formats, not model families. A quantization scheme describes numerical representation. A runtime executes a supported artifact. Mixing up these layers causes avoidable compatibility failures.

Open weights means weights are available under some terms. Open source is a broader licensing claim. Access does not automatically permit every commercial use or redistribution.||Hosted models reduce infrastructure work; local models give more operational control. Compare the whole system: quality, latency, resources, licenses, privacy, and maintenance. Test your own tasks before committing.

Memory capacity determines whether model weights and runtime state can fit. Memory bandwidth affects how quickly data moves. Compute capability affects how fast operations execute. These are related but distinct constraints.||A model that loads may still be too slow for interactive use. Longer context and multiple requests increase memory demands beyond the weight file. Unified memory and discrete GPU memory have different operating tradeoffs.

A local chat interface is not necessarily the inference engine. The interface talks to a runtime, which uses hardware backends and drivers to execute a model. A local API server makes that capability available to other local software.||CPU offloading moves some work away from the GPU and can help a model fit, often with a performance cost. Check architecture and quantization support before downloading.

Start with a hardware inventory and a small compatible model. Record the exact model revision, template, runtime version, prompt, output limit, and sampling settings. Change one thing at a time.||Use fixed prompts to create a baseline. Measure loading separately from generation. A reproducible modest result is more informative than an impressive number with unknown settings.

Out-of-memory failures can come from weights, caches, activations, or concurrency. Bad output can come from a mismatched chat template rather than poor weights. Slow responses can reflect CPU offload or unsupported acceleration.||Local software may still call remote services for some features. Inspect the actual data flow. Binding a server to localhost limits network exposure; binding to every interface changes who may reach it.

Numerical precision is how finely a value is represented. Quantization stores values using a more compact representation, reducing weight memory and sometimes accelerating supported computation.||Storage precision and compute precision can differ. A four-bit model is not necessarily performing every operation in four bits. Lower precision may damage some capabilities more than others.

Post-training quantization transforms an already trained model. Quantization-aware training incorporates the effects of lower precision during training. Calibration examples can help select representations that preserve important behavior.||Weights, activations, and the KV cache can be quantized separately. The choice affects different memory costs. Always evaluate the configuration you will actually deploy.

Labels such as a GGUF quantization variant, GPTQ, AWQ, or NF4 describe different representation and tooling choices. They are not interchangeable downloads for every engine.||Two four-bit artifacts can have different quality, memory overhead, and hardware kernels. Read the runtime's compatibility documentation and benchmark the actual combination.

Distillation trains a student model using guidance from another model. Pruning removes selected parameters or structures. Sparsity means some values or operations can be omitted. Quantization changes precision.||These methods can be combined, but compression does not automatically produce acceleration. Hardware and software must exploit the changed representation.

Prefill processes the prompt and prepares state for generation. Decode generates subsequent tokens. Time to first token captures how long the user waits before output begins; output speed describes the later stream.||A long prompt may delay the first token even when generation is fast. Report both phases when comparing systems. Streaming improves perceived responsiveness without necessarily reducing total work.

The KV cache stores intermediate attention information so previous tokens do not need the same computation repeated during decoding. Its memory generally grows with context and concurrent sequences.||Prefix caching can reuse shared prompt computation across compatible requests. This is not semantic memory: it does not decide which past facts should be remembered or corrected.

Batching processes multiple requests together to use hardware efficiently. Continuous batching allows requests to join or leave as generation proceeds. Chunked prefill breaks large prompt work into pieces.||Speculative decoding proposes tokens cheaply and verifies them with a target model. Optimizations involve tradeoffs: higher throughput can increase a particular user's waiting time.

A serving system manages more than inference. It queues requests, controls concurrency, handles cancellation, applies limits, and reports failures. Without backpressure, a busy service can exhaust memory or create long queues.||Choose interactive or batch settings according to the task. A nightly report and a conversational tutor have different latency requirements.

Prompting changes instructions. Retrieval supplies evidence. Fine-tuning changes learned behavior through further training. Continued pretraining extends broad modeling on new material; supervised fine-tuning uses task examples.||Start with the least complex approach that solves the problem. Frequently changing factual documents usually need retrieval. Repeated formatting or behavioral patterns may be candidates for fine-tuning.

Training examples must match the format used by the trainer and model. Chat templates, turn boundaries, truncation, and which tokens contribute to loss all affect what is learned.||Reserve test cases before experimentation. Remove near-duplicates across splits. A dataset full of polished but incorrect synthetic answers can teach confident mistakes.

Establish a baseline, prepare data, run a tiny sanity check, train, validate, save, and evaluate on held-out examples. Record settings so the result can be reproduced.||Training needs memory for more than weights: activations, gradients, and optimizer state can dominate. Gradient accumulation and checkpointing trade time and memory in different ways.

Training a tiny model from scratch can demonstrate the lifecycle on ordinary hardware. It does not recreate the broad knowledge of a large pretrained model. Adapting a small existing model is often the more useful experiment.||Choose a narrow task, monitor validation, and stop if performance degrades. Report what changed on unrelated tasks as well as the target task.

LoRA keeps the base model frozen and learns a relatively small set of added parameters. These low-rank updates adjust selected parts of the model without updating every original weight.||Rank controls part of the adapter's capacity; target modules decide where it acts. More rank is not automatically better. Data quality, training settings, and evaluation still matter.

QLoRA trains adapters while keeping a quantized base model frozen. This reduces the memory needed for the base weights during adaptation. Computation can use higher precision than the stored weights.||It does not mean all model weights are directly trained in four-bit precision. The trainable adapter, runtime state, and compute buffers still have their own memory requirements.

An adapter is tied to a compatible base model and configuration. Saving only the adapter does not create a standalone copy of the full model. Record the base revision, tokenizer, template, and settings.||Some workflows merge the adapter into base weights. Merging or re-quantizing can change deployment behavior, so evaluate the exported artifact rather than assuming equivalence.

Parameter-efficient adaptation includes several families. Prompt tuning learns continuous prompt representations; prefix methods add learned state; adapter methods introduce trainable components. These are not the same as manually writing a better prompt.||Full fine-tuning offers broader changes at greater resource cost. Choose by measured task benefit and regressions, not by the newest acronym.

Instruction tuning uses examples of requested behavior. Preference training uses comparisons, such as which of two answers is better. RLHF uses human feedback in a reinforcement-learning pipeline; RLAIF uses AI feedback in some roles.||DPO directly optimizes from preference comparisons under its formulation. Human preference, factual truth, and safety are overlapping but different goals.

A policy chooses actions; a rollout is an interaction trajectory; a reward scores outcomes. For a model, an action may be generated text or a tool decision.||A reward is only a proxy. If the score rewards length, the system may become verbose rather than helpful. Verifiable tasks can provide stronger checks, but scoring rules still need scrutiny.

A student model can learn from a teacher's outputs or other signals. Synthetic examples can expand coverage and rejection sampling can retain better candidates.||The teacher can be wrong. Repeatedly recycling unchecked synthetic content can narrow diversity and reinforce mistakes. Use independent validation and keep evaluation data separate.

Data parallelism divides examples across devices. Tensor and pipeline parallelism split model computation. Expert parallelism distributes experts. Sharding divides large training state.||More devices introduce communication and recovery costs. A distributed job needs consistent configuration, checkpoints, and monitoring; adding GPUs is not a guaranteed proportional speedup.

Keyword search is strong when exact terms matter. Semantic search uses embeddings to retrieve related meaning even when words differ. Hybrid search combines signals; a reranker reassesses shortlisted results.||A vector database stores and searches representations. It does not independently decide whether a source is true, current, or authorized for a particular user.

A RAG pipeline parses documents, splits them into chunks, indexes them, retrieves candidates, and supplies selected evidence to generation. Metadata preserves source identity, dates, and access rules.||Chunking too narrowly can remove context; too broadly can bury relevant details. Citations must point to evidence that actually supports the answer.

Query rewriting can make a question easier to retrieve for. Multi-hop tasks need several pieces of evidence. Structured data may be better queried through a database than converted into prose chunks.||Knowledge graphs represent explicit relationships. Graph-based retrieval is useful for some connected questions, but adds maintenance and complexity. Compare it with simpler retrieval first.

Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Did the relevant source appear in the candidates? Did the answer use it correctly? These are different tests.||Updates and deletions must reach the index. A source can be accurate historically but wrong for today's policy. Apply permissions before exposing retrieved content.

An API defines how software requests a capability and receives results. Requests include inputs and often authentication; responses include output or errors. Streaming delivers pieces as they become available.||Timeouts and rate limits are normal operating conditions. The user interface should explain what happened and preserve input rather than pretending an empty answer is success.

Structured output follows a defined shape such as JSON fields. Tool calling produces a request for software to execute an operation. Both require validation.||A valid date string can still be the wrong date. Check meaning as well as structure. The model's proposed tool arguments should not bypass application authorization.

MCP standardizes how AI applications connect to external capabilities. Hosts manage clients, clients connect to servers, and servers expose supported tools, resources, or prompts.||A protocol is not permission. The application still needs authentication, access controls, and safe execution. MCP does not replace every underlying service API.

A write operation may succeed even if the response is lost. Blindly retrying can create a duplicate booking or payment. Idempotency keys and status checks help distinguish failure from uncertain completion.||Use read-only operations when sufficient. After a change, verify the external state before reporting success. Keep an audit trail for consequential actions.

A workflow follows predefined paths. An agent can choose actions dynamically toward a goal. Both may use the same model and tools. Autonomy is a design choice.||An agent needs a stopping rule, budget, and evidence of success. For a predictable task, a fixed workflow can be easier to test and more reliable.

The harness is the software around the model. It builds context, dispatches tools, records state, handles errors, and decides how execution continues. Permissions and cancellation belong here too.||A weak harness can turn a good model into an unreliable application. Fixing lost tool results or missing recovery state may matter more than changing models.

Skills package reusable guidance and sometimes scripts or resources. Subagents divide work and may use isolated contexts. A coordinator combines results.||Parallelism creates coordination costs: duplicated work, stale assumptions, and conflicting edits. Define ownership, input/output contracts, and completion checks before adding agents.

Coding and browser agents act in environments that change. A command can fail, an element can move, or a page can require a login. The agent must inspect feedback and revise its plan.||Durable execution saves enough state to recover after interruption. The final message is not proof of completion; verify files, tests, or external results.

Vision systems can classify an image, locate objects, segment regions, read text, or answer questions about visual content. These are different tasks with different error patterns.||Small text, crowded scenes, and spatial relationships can be difficult. Ask the system to separate what is directly visible from what it infers.

Image generators learn patterns that can produce images conditioned on text or other inputs. Diffusion progressively transforms noise; flow-matching methods learn related transformation dynamics. Some systems use autoregressive generation.||Seeds and sampling settings influence results, but exact reproducibility also depends on software and hardware. Visual appeal does not prove factual accuracy.

Inpainting edits a region; outpainting extends a canvas; image-to-image uses an input image as a starting condition. Reference conditioning and control signals guide composition or identity.||An image LoRA adapts a model for certain patterns, such as a style. It is not a guarantee of exact identity preservation. Compare edits against the original intent.

Video adds time. A frame can look good while motion between frames is inconsistent. Understanding systems may sample frames and miss brief events. Generation must maintain identity, geometry, and motion over time.||A world model attempts to represent aspects of an environment's dynamics. Plausible simulated behavior is not proof of physically valid prediction.

Speech recognition converts audio to text. Diarization estimates who spoke when. Language identification and timestamps add different metadata. Noise, accents, and uncommon names can cause errors.||A readable transcript may silently replace an unfamiliar name with a familiar one. Verify details before using the transcript to take action.

Text-to-speech generates spoken audio from text. Prosody includes rhythm, stress, and intonation. Dubbing also requires translation choices, timing, and often synchronization with video.||Voice likeness raises consent and provenance questions. Evaluate intelligibility and meaning, not only how natural the voice sounds.

A real-time assistant must decide when you started, paused, interrupted, or finished speaking. Voice activity detection and turn-taking influence whether it feels responsive.||A pipeline may transcribe, reason, then synthesize; another model may process audio more directly. Measure the full interaction, including interruptions and recovery from mishearing.

Robotics connects perception, planning, and control to physical consequences. Imitation learning learns from demonstrations; reinforcement learning uses rewards from interaction. Simulators make some experiments cheaper.||The real world differs from simulation. Sensors, friction, delays, and unexpected people matter. On-device AI and federated learning address different deployment and data-distribution concerns.

An evaluation starts with a task and a definition of success. Collect representative cases, establish a baseline, and keep some examples untouched while improving the system.||A model judge can help review outputs, but may share biases with the model being evaluated. Human review and deterministic checks remain useful.

Accuracy counts correct predictions overall. Precision asks how many positive predictions were right; recall asks how many real positives were found. The right balance depends on consequences.||For serving, averages can hide slow outliers. Latency percentiles and cost per successful task can tell you more than raw token speed or cost per request.

Trace a failure through the pipeline: source data, retrieval, prompt assembly, model, tool execution, and interface. Locate the first incorrect step before changing the system.||An ablation removes or changes one component to test its contribution. Changing many things at once can improve results while leaving you unsure why.

A paper's contribution depends on the problem, baseline, dataset, evaluation, and resource budget. Read limitations and ablations, not just the headline score.||Contamination occurs when evaluation material leaks into training or tuning. A leaderboard improvement may not transfer to your workload. Seek reproducible evidence.

Prompt injection is untrusted content trying to redirect the application. It may be hidden inside a retrieved document or tool output. Poisoning alters data used for learning or retrieval.||A system with powerful tools can turn a text misunderstanding into an external action. Map the information and action boundaries, not only the prompt.

Least privilege gives a component only the access it needs. Sandboxing limits what execution can affect. Authorization checks decide which actions a user is allowed to take.||A source document cannot grant itself permission. Enforce boundaries in software and infrastructure. Instructions to 'be safe' are not equivalent to access control.

Retention describes how long data remains stored. Training use describes whether it may help improve models. Sharing describes who can access it. These are separate questions.||Bias, accessibility, attribution, and consent affect real users. Check current provider settings and relevant legal requirements rather than assuming every account has the same policy.

Governance creates a record of intended use, known limits, tests, ownership, and incident handling. Red teaming actively looks for ways a system can fail.||A successful defense against one example does not establish overall safety. Monitor actual deployment, define release criteria, and keep a response plan for unexpected behavior.

Start with the user's job, not the model. Decide where AI helps, where deterministic logic is sufficient, and where a person should review an outcome.||A useful interface communicates uncertainty and offers recovery. A system that occasionally refuses or falls back can be more useful than one that confidently invents a result.

Production changes include new models, prompts, data, and tools. Version them so a regression can be traced. Test before release and retain a rollback path.||Monitor task success as well as uptime. A service can be technically available while producing worse answers after a data or model change.

Total cost includes inference, infrastructure, storage, engineering, monitoring, and failures. A cheap request that needs repeated correction may cost more per successful task.||Local, cloud, and hybrid approaches distribute these costs differently. Compare realistic workloads, including peak usage and maintenance, before choosing.

Integration means explaining the whole path from user input to verified outcome. Defend each component against a simpler alternative. Document what you measured and what remains uncertain.||New terminology becomes manageable when you ask where it fits: data, model, adaptation, inference, context, tools, evaluation, or deployment. Extend the map with evidence rather than chasing every release.
checks: Which part actually executes a web search?
The model can request a search, but application software performs it and returns the result.
Held-out examples test whether learning transfers beyond the examples used for tuning.
Tokenization encodes input; it does not verify meaning or remember a user.
Independent evidence or a reproducible test
The same model can repeat its mistake. Check evidence outside the claim.
Which can survive a chat through application storage?
The current KV cache in every app
The application must store and later supply persistent information; it is not a weight update.
What must match a model checkpoint?
The model expects a specific encoding and message format.
A model fits in memory. What follows?
Compute, bandwidth, offloading, caches, and context also affect performance.
Lower precision can reduce resource use, with possible quality and compatibility tradeoffs.
Prefill processes input; decode generates subsequent tokens.
What is often best for frequently changing facts?
Retrieval can supply current evidence without requiring weight updates.
In typical LoRA training, what is frozen?
LoRA trains added parameters while keeping the base frozen.
Can a higher reward score hide worse behavior?
Yes, a proxy can be gamed
Optimization can exploit flaws in a reward rule rather than improve the intended behavior.
A cited answer is wrong. What should you inspect?
A citation may refer to irrelevant, stale, or misinterpreted evidence.
A write request times out. What should happen first?
A timeout can leave completion uncertain; blind retries can duplicate actions.
The harness coordinates the model's work and its interaction with the environment.
A video model samples frames. What might happen?
It misses an event between samples
It updates its weights on the video
Sampling trades coverage for processing cost and can omit brief events.
Does a correct transcript prove a successful voice action?
No, interpretation and execution may fail
Yes, transcription is the whole system
Yes, if the voice sounds natural
The full voice pipeline must be checked beyond speech recognition.
What makes a comparison more credible?
Fixed tests and a clear baseline
Controlled comparisons make it easier to attribute the change and assess coverage.
Can a retrieved page grant permission to send private data?
No, authorization belongs to the application
Yes, if it is very long
Untrusted content is evidence to inspect, not an authority to change permissions.
Which is most useful for product economics?
Retries, failures, infrastructure, and review affect the real cost of delivering value.
